page.meta_description: A client asks whether you use AI with their data. Build a truthful one-page AI statement and answer letter, in English or Dutch, from what you have confirmed.
page.title: A client asks how you use AI with their data
page.lead: Often there is a renewal or a new contract waiting. Here is what clients ask, why they ask it, and a builder that turns what your firm has confirmed into a one-page statement and a short letter.
page.answer: Tell them which AI tools you use and under which accounts, what may go into them, who checks the output, and what you are still checking. Say only what you have confirmed, and keep what the vendor promises apart from what you checked yourself. The builder below writes the statement and the letter that way, in English or Dutch.
page.asks_intro: Client questionnaires and contract clauses come back to the same points. Here they are in the clients' own words, and where your statement answers each one.

asks.q: Do you use AI on our data, or only for your own back office?
asks.where: The AI tools you use; what goes in

asks.q: Which AI tools, from which vendors?
Will our data be used to train the AI?
asks.where: Per tool: training, and what the vendor states

asks.q: Where is our data stored, and how long is it kept?
Who checks the output, and who is responsible if it is wrong?
Are your staff trained to use it?
Is the AI vendor a sub-processor we approved?
Can we ask you not to use AI on our work?

why.title: If you are their processor
why.text: Under the GDPR a processor may not engage another processor without the client's prior written authorisation, specific or general. Under a general authorisation it must tell the client about a new one, so the client can object. An AI vendor that processes the client's personal data for you is such a sub-processor.

why.title: Their contracts
why.text: Model contract clauses for AI, published for public buyers by the European Commission's procurement community, ask suppliers not to use client data for anything but the agreed work, to delete it on request, to keep a person watching for over-reliance on AI output, and to give information on request. A client's own contract may use similar wording.

why.title: Not the AI Act, mostly
why.text: Article 50 of the AI Act, which applies from 2 August 2026, sets transparency duties for providers of AI systems, and for deployers of emotion recognition, of deep fakes, and of AI-written text published to inform the public on matters of public interest. Using ChatGPT or Copilot on client work is none of those. A KvK page explains those duties; it doesn't answer your client's question.

page.gap_text: Your statement covers the tools your firm arranged. It can't cover what staff use on their own, and that is usually what the client is really asking about. If you aren't sure, the statement says so, as an open point. The AI accounts guide has a 20-minute check you can do yourself. Noxiom's fixed-price AI usage review finds out properly, from an anonymous staff survey, your admin screens and your billing, so the next statement has no open point there.

faq.q: Does the AI Act require us to tell clients that we use AI?
faq.a: Not for ordinary internal use. Article 50 sets transparency duties for providers of AI systems, such as the makers of chatbots, and for deployers of emotion recognition, deep fakes, and AI-written text published to inform the public on matters of public interest. Using an AI tool on client work isn't one of those. What you owe a client comes from your contract with them, from the GDPR where you are their processor, and from your professional rules. Separately, Article 4 asks firms that use AI systems to see to their staff's AI literacy.

faq.q: We are the client's processor. Do we need their permission for an AI tool?
faq.a: A processor may not engage another processor without the controller's prior specific or general written authorisation. Under a general authorisation, it must tell the controller about new ones so the controller can object. An AI vendor that processes your client's personal data is such a sub-processor. Check what your processing agreement with the client says, and put the vendor on the list you give them.

faq.q: Can we tell the client the tool is GDPR compliant?
faq.a: The statement doesn't say that, and we advise against it. Say what you checked: the agreement with the vendor, the training setting, the storage location, and what the vendor states, with the date. Whether your use meets the GDPR depends on how you use the tool, not on the tool alone.

faq.q: What if we don't know which AI tools our staff use?
faq.a: Then the statement says so, as an open point. A statement that claims more than the firm knows does more harm than an honest open point, especially if the client later finds out. The 20-minute check in the AI accounts guide is a first step.

faq.q: Why does the statement keep what the vendor says apart from what we checked?
faq.a: Because they are different claims. "Training is off: we checked the setting" is your firm's fact. "The vendor says it doesn't train on business data by default" is the vendor's promise. Your client's lawyer reads them differently, and you can only vouch for the first.

faq.q: Does this page send or keep what we enter?
faq.a: No. The builder runs in your browser. It sends nothing and stores nothing; when you close the tab, it is gone. Save the statement as Word, or your answers as a .json file to continue later.

assistant.intro: Rather talk it through, or on your phone? An AI assistant can ask you the questions and give you the answers as one block of JSON. You paste it back here, check it, and save.
assistant.caution: Use your firm's work account for this. Don't give it client names or client data: the questions are about your firm's own setup.
assistant.prompt: Help me fill in my firm's AI facts, for an AI statement to clients. The questions and the allowed answers are at https://noxiom.com/data/firm-ai-facts.schema.json (the same list is on https://noxiom.com/client-asks-about-ai under "For AI assistants"). Ask me the questions one at a time, in plain words, and offer the allowed answers. For each AI account the firm provides, also ask the short questions about it (tool_facts). Only record what I have confirmed: if I'm not sure, use the "not sure" answer or leave it out; don't guess, and don't fill in what a vendor promises as if it were my firm's fact. Don't ask for client names or client data. When we're done, give me the whole result as one JSON code block, so I can paste it back into the page.
